items.question: Where is chlorophyll found in the cells of a leaf?
items.explanation: The green dots seen in some leaf cells are organelles called chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll.

items.question: In the starch-test activity with a variegated leaf, why is the plant first left in darkness for three days?
options: To use up the starch already in its leaves
To remove water from the leaves
items.explanation: Keeping the plant in the dark for three days uses up its starch, so any starch found after six hours of sunlight must have been made by photosynthesis.

items.question: In what form do plants take up nitrogen from the soil?
options: Only as nitrogen gas from the air
As inorganic nitrates or nitrites, or organic compounds made by bacteria
items.explanation: Nitrogen, needed to make proteins, is taken up as inorganic nitrates or nitrites, or as organic compounds prepared by bacteria from atmospheric nitrogen.

items.question: What are stomata?
options: Tiny pores on the surface of leaves
items.explanation: Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves through which massive amounts of gaseous exchange take place for photosynthesis.

items.question: What happens to the stomatal pore when the guard cells shrink?
items.explanation: Guard cells control the pore: it opens when they swell with water and closes when they shrink.

items.question: Apart from the leaves, across which surfaces does exchange of gases occur in plants?
items.explanation: Most gaseous exchange happens through the stomata, but exchange of gases also occurs across the surface of stems and roots.

items.question: How does Amoeba take in food?
options: Cilia move food to one fixed spot on the cell
Temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface fuse over the food, forming a food vacuole
Through a mouth and a gut
items.explanation: Amoeba uses temporary finger-like extensions of its cell surface, which fuse over the food particle to form a food vacuole. Moving food to a fixed spot with cilia describes Paramoecium.

items.question: In Paramoecium, how is food moved to the specific spot where it is taken in?
options: By the movement of cilia covering the cell surface
By diffusion through the whole surface
items.explanation: Paramoecium has a definite shape and takes in food at a specific spot; cilia covering the whole cell surface move the food there.

items.question: Which organisms are named in the chapter as heterotrophs?
items.explanation: Heterotrophs use complex substances made by others; the chapter names animals and fungi. Green plants and some bacteria are autotrophs.

items.question: What moves food forward along the alimentary canal?
options: Rhythmic contraction of muscles in the lining of the canal
items.explanation: Muscles in the wall of the canal contract in rhythmic waves (peristalsis) that push food onward through the whole gut.

items.question: What protects the inner lining of the stomach from its acid?
items.explanation: The gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus; the mucus protects the inner lining of the stomach from the acid under normal conditions.

items.question: The enzymes in intestinal juice finally convert fats into:
items.explanation: Intestinal juice enzymes finally convert proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates to glucose, and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.

items.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?
items.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains trypsin, which digests proteins, and lipase, which breaks down emulsified fats.

items.question: Which kind of respiration releases more energy?
items.explanation: Aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen, releases a lot more energy than the anaerobic process.

items.question: How does the chapter describe ATP?
options: The energy currency for most cellular processes
items.explanation: The energy released in respiration is used to make ATP, which fuels activities such as muscle contraction, protein synthesis and conduction of nerve impulses.

items.question: When pyruvate is broken down using oxygen, it gives carbon dioxide and which other product?
items.explanation: In the mitochondria, aerobic break-down of the three-carbon pyruvate gives three molecules of carbon dioxide; the other product is water.

items.question: Why is the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms much faster than in terrestrial organisms?
options: The amount of dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared to oxygen in air
Water contains more oxygen than air
Aquatic organisms do not need oxygen
items.explanation: Water holds much less dissolved oxygen than air, so aquatic organisms such as fish must breathe much faster.

items.question: What stops the air-passage in the throat from collapsing?
items.explanation: Rings of cartilage in the throat keep the air-passage open. Fine hairs and mucus filter the air in the nostrils.

items.question: During the day, why is there no release of carbon dioxide from the leaves of a plant?
options: Plants do not respire during the day
The carbon dioxide made in respiration is used up for photosynthesis
The stomata stay closed all day
Carbon dioxide is stored as starch in the roots
items.explanation: Plants respire all the time, but during the day the carbon dioxide from respiration is used for photosynthesis, so oxygen release is the main exchange. At night, carbon dioxide is given out.

items.question: Why do the lungs always contain a residual volume of air?
options: So that there is enough time for oxygen to be absorbed and carbon dioxide to be released
items.explanation: Keeping a residual volume of air in the lungs during the breathing cycle gives enough time for oxygen to be absorbed and carbon dioxide to be released.

items.question: What is the job of platelets?
options: To plug leaks by helping blood to clot at points of injury
items.explanation: Platelets circulate in the blood and plug leaks by helping blood clot at injuries, which limits blood loss and loss of pressure.

items.question: Why do the ventricles of the heart have thicker muscular walls than the atria?
options: They receive blood from the veins
They pump blood into various organs
items.explanation: Ventricles have to pump blood out to various organs, so they have thicker muscular walls than the atria, which only collect blood.

items.question: How many chambers does a fish heart have, and how many times does blood pass through it in one cycle?
items.explanation: Fish have two-chambered hearts: blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated, and passes directly to the body, so it goes through the heart only once per cycle. Other vertebrates have double circulation.

items.question: What is lymph?
options: A colourless fluid similar to plasma that contains less protein
A red fluid rich in haemoglobin
A digestive juice from the pancreas
Urine before it reaches the bladder
items.explanation: Lymph (tissue fluid) forms from plasma that escapes through capillary pores; it is like plasma but colourless with less protein, and it carries absorbed fat and drains excess fluid back into the blood.

items.question: What is transpiration?
options: Water evaporating as vapour from the leaves and other parts above the ground
items.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant; it creates the suction that pulls water up the xylem.

items.question: Besides helping the upward movement of water and minerals, what else does transpiration help with?
items.explanation: Transpiration helps absorb and move water and minerals upwards, and it also helps in temperature regulation.

items.question: How do root cells start the movement of water from the soil into the root?
options: By actively taking up ions, so that water moves in from the soil
items.explanation: Root cells actively take up ions, creating a concentration difference between root and soil; water moves into the root to eliminate this difference.

items.question: Which substances in the initial filtrate are selectively re-absorbed as urine flows along the kidney tube?
options: Glucose, amino acids, salts and much of the water
items.explanation: As the filtrate moves along the tubule, useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water) are taken back selectively.

items.question: What is Bowman's capsule?
options: The cup-shaped end of a coiled tube that collects the filtrate
The tube that carries urine to the bladder
The muscle that controls the urethra
items.explanation: In each nephron, a knot of thin-walled capillaries sits inside Bowman's capsule, the cup-like start of a coiled tubule, which catches the filtrate.

items.question: How is an artificial kidney (haemodialysis) different from a real kidney?
options: It does not use the patient's blood
items.explanation: In dialysis, wastes diffuse from the blood into dialysing fluid, similar to the kidney, but nothing is re-absorbed.

items.question: Which substance can be thought of as a waste product of photosynthesis?
items.explanation: Plants release the oxygen produced in photosynthesis, so oxygen can be thought of as a waste product of it.

Excreting some wastes into the soil
